title: Lior and the Radiators
premise: Theo Villalobos has spent three years writing postcards to Marisol Reyes at an address that burned down in the Lior district fire, never sending the one sentence that matters. When a demolition crew uncovers a box of undelivered letters behind a wardrobe — letters Marisol wrote to him, returned unopened — Theo learns she survived the fire and vanished on purpose. Tracking her through the city's radiator-repair shops, where a loose community of burn survivors called the Radiators took her in, he must confront what his silence cost her: the night of the fire, he chose to protect his brother's secret over warning her family. The novel ends not with forgiveness granted but with Theo staying — repairing radiators beside her through one long winter — as Marisol finally reads aloud the last unsent postcard and lets him begin again as a stranger.
about_author: Quentin Thornbury is the pen name of a former postal clerk who spent a decade sorting dead letters in a coastal city much like Lior. Their fiction explores the geography of things we almost say, and this is their second novel.

chapters.title: The Address That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He writes his 214th postcard to a burned lot, narrating his ritual of saying everything except the truth. A demolition notice appears on the fence next door. The beat is quiet dread: the past is about to be physically excavated.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The crew finds a tin box wedged behind a wardrobe: forty-one letters addressed to Theo, all returned unopened, postmarked across three years before the fire. He recognizes Marisol's handwriting instantly. The beat is vertigo — she was writing to him all along.

chapters.title: What the Letters Don't Say
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, intercut with excerpts. He reads the early letters, warm and ordinary, and understands they stop mid-sentence the month his own began. The emotional beat is shame sharpening into resolve: he will find her.

chapters.title: The Radiator Man of Delmore Street
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Following a repair sticker inside the box, he finds Aurelio's Radiator Works, a cluttered shop that functions as an unofficial archive for people the fire displaced. Aurelio is wary, testing him with questions. Beat: first door opening, first resistance.

chapters.title: People Who Burned
chapters.summary: Aurelio's POV. He remembers Marisol arriving winter after the fire, hands scarred, refusing to give a surname. He explains the Radiators — survivors who fix heat for each other because no institution would. Beat: Theo learns belonging can be built from damage.

chapters.title: The Brother's Version
chapters.summary: Theo visits his brother Ruben, now sober and churchgoing, who begs him to let the fire stay buried. Flashback reveals the truth partially: Ruben's debt started it, and Theo covered for him instead of warning the Reyeses upstairs. Beat: complicity named aloud for the first time.

chapters.title: Postcard Weather
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, years earlier. She writes letter twelve, describing the neighborhood's small graces and her hope that Theo will answer. Dramatic irony aches: readers know he never will. Beat: tenderness on the edge of abandonment.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Fixes Heat
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He spots Marisol across a market square but cannot approach; she moves like someone practiced at being unfindable. He buys a broken radiator just to have a reason to return to the shop where she works Tuesdays. Beat: cowardice dressed as patience.

chapters.title: Tuesday Repairs
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. A stranger brings in a radiator deliberately broken — she can tell — and she plays along, curious and guarded. Their conversation is all subtext about heat, cold, and starting over. Beat: two people circling a fire neither names.

chapters.title: Forty-One Envelopes
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He reads the final letters, where her tone turns from hope to fury to something colder than either. The last one says only: 'I saw you that night. You looked right at the window.' Beat: the floor drops out — she knows.

chapters.title: The Night, Told Twice
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, flashback. The fire rendered twice: Theo's version, where he froze protecting Ruben; Marisol's version, where she watched him look away. Neither is fully reliable. Beat: the reader becomes the judge Theo fears.

chapters.title: Confession as Craft
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Unable to speak it, he does what he does best: he writes. A full confession, sealed, left with Aurelio marked 'for when she asks.' Beat: the art of almost saying it, finally overcome by paper.

chapters.title: She Reads It Standing Up
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She finds the envelope, reads it alone in the shop, and does not cry or rage — she simply closes early and walks the frozen streets until dawn. Beat: grief with nowhere to perform itself.

chapters.title: The Radiators Vote
chapters.summary: Ensemble scene, mostly Aurelio's POV. The community debates whether Theo belongs among them; some lost family in the fire. Marisol refuses to decide for them. Beat: justice outside the law takes the shape of a difficult room.

chapters.title: Probation by Wrench
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The verdict: he may stay and work, unpaid, unseen, until winter ends. He learns the trade badly, burns his hand, and is tended by the very people he wronged. Beat: humiliation as the beginning of repair.

chapters.title: Ruben Comes to the Shop
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Ruben arrives seeking Theo, and Marisol faces the man whose debt killed her parents' home while Theo watches, unable to intervene. She chooses not to expose him — yet. Beat: mercy withheld as leverage, power shifting to her.

chapters.title: Thaw Faults
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Late winter; pipes burst across the district and the Radiators work around the clock. Exhausted, side by side, he and Marisol talk about anything but the fire — and it feels, dangerously, like friendship. Beat: warmth that both distrust.

chapters.title: The Photograph Stranger
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She shows Theo the old photographs from the box and demands he forgive the stranger in them — himself, younger, afraid — before she ever can. He resists, then breaks. Beat: the novel's thesis spoken aloud: self-forgiveness precedes absolution.

chapters.title: What Justice Looks Like Here
chapters.summary: Ensemble, Theo's POV. The Radiators convene a final reckoning: no police, no court — Theo must read every one of Marisol's forty-one letters aloud to the room. Beat: public truth-telling as the community's law.

chapters.title: Letter Forty-One
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. As Theo reads her last, coldest letter, she interrupts and finishes it herself — revealing its true ending, which she'd never mailed: a question, not an accusation. Beat: climax; the wound and the want turn out to share a page.

chapters.title: The Last Unsent Postcard
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Spring. He gives Marisol postcard 214, the one that always said too much. She reads it silently, folds it away, and says only: 'Start over. Introduce yourself.' Beat: forgiveness not granted but made possible.

chapters.title: Introductions
chapters.summary: Shared POV, brief alternating paragraphs. In the shop, amid steam and solder, Theo extends a hand: 'Theo Villalobos. I'm learning to fix heat.' Marisol takes it. The Radiators keep working around them. Beat: resolution — belonging rebuilt from ash, one honest sentence at a time.
